newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Labour votes, aiming to unseat Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Labour votes, aiming to unseat Netanyahu.

text.p: Israel's main opposition Labour party, hungry to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government, votes on Tuesday to choose a new leader with ex-army chief Ehud Barak tipped to succeed Shimon Peres at the helm.

The leadership vote marks a milestone for Labour, a passing of the political torch from former prime minister Peres, 73, and his slain predecessor Yitzhak Rabin, whose rival camps ruled the often contentious party for nearly a quarter-century.
The heavily favoured Barak, 55, has cast himself as heir to Rabin's warrior-turned-peacemaker mantle.
"I see myself as his follower and the one to continue his legacy," Barak told a news conference on Monday.
The winner of the Tuesday contest is expected to face Netanyahu in national elections slated for the year 2000.

Echoing Rabin, who spearheaded Arab-Israeli talks until a ultra-nationalist Jew gunned him down after a 1995 peace rally, Barak said Labour was "committed to take calculated risks in the Middle East in order to achieve peace".
The voting closes at 1900 GMT and exit polls are expected to predict the winner soon afterwards. Only Labour Party members can vote.
Opinion polls have shown Barak neck and neck with Netanyahu, 47, whose first year in office has been buffeted by peacemaking crises and shadowed by corruption allegations.

Facing Barak when polls open at 0700 GMT will be Peres's longtime protege Yossi Beilin, 48, the bookish prophet of Labour peace policies; Shlomo Ben-Ami, 53, a Moroccan-born novice politician with roots both in academia and among the disadvantaged; and Ephraim Sneh, 52, a physician and brigadier general before he served Rabin and Peres as health minister.
Pundits said Barak needs more than 50 percent of the vote to consolidate his position in Labour, which he joined barely two years ago after shedding the uniform of Israel's most decorated soldier.
Long before entering public life, Barak was a near-legendary military figure -- bold, aloof, and brilliant. He was Netanyahu's commander when both served in an elite commando unit.
The military credentials have helped catapault self-described centrist Barak to prominence in a country where security remains the paramount -- if not the sole -- issue in election campaigns.
Barak joined Rabin's cabinet as interior minister in 1995, succeeding Peres as foreign minister when the Labour veteran took the reins of government following the Rabin assassination.
Netanyahu edged Peres in an upset election victory in 1996, in part by characterising the Nobel peace laureate as soft on security.
Labour's primary campaign has been called unusually gentlemanly, the candidates mindful of avoiding the infighting that kept Labour in the electoral cold for much of the last two decades.

The relative calm was broken last month, when Barak's forces quashed a bid by Peres backers to appoint the veteran leader honorary party president. Peres has stayed out of the fray, refraining from endorsing Beilin, whom Rabin was once quoted as dubbing "Peres's poodle."

Widely respected by party regulars for charting breakthrough peace moves with Israel's Arab neighbours, Beilin has had to battle critics who argue he lacks the mix of charisma and killer instinct that voters in the Jewish state traditionally favour.
Beilin may also be dogged by his association with Peres, whose image as the serial loser of Israeli politics is one the party would dearly like to shake.
Analysts have said Beilin must garner at least a quarter of the total vote to be seen as a significant challenger to Barak for future party leadership.

Ben-Ami, little known before he entered the Labour race, can cement a place in party leadership by reaping at least 10 percent of the vote, Israeli media said. The square-jawed, somewhat reserved Sneh is given little chance of success.
